Awaiting the cancelled tasks is what lets each job's `finally` blocks and `async with` cleanup actually execute before the original exception is re-raised. A bare `raise` propagates the original cause.\n\n## Verified Ctrl+C behavior (from the end-to-end run)\n\nWith 5 jobs and `max_concurrent=2`, sending SIGINT once produced:\n```\nstart 0\nstart 1\ncleanup 0      ← both started jobs' cleanup ran\ncleanup 1\nmain exiting: CancelledError\n```\nSo cleanup **does** run on interrupt. ✅ A second Ctrl+C forces an immediate exit (standard asyncio behavior).\n\n## Things worth knowing\n\n- **Fail-fast on errors:** if one job raises, the remaining jobs are cancelled (and cleaned up) and that original exception is re-raised. Jobs that were still waiting on the semaphore (never started) don't run their body/cleanup — there's nothing for them to clean up.\n- **`max_concurrent < 1`** raises `ValueError`.\n- The traceback you see on Ctrl+C (`CancelledError` → `KeyboardInterrupt`) is the standard `asyncio.run` output, not a bug. All jobs are scheduled up front and self-throttle by acquiring a slot, so at most `max_concurrent` run at once.\n- **Graceful interrupt (your main concern):** the jobs are awaited via `asyncio.gather`. When a `KeyboardInterrupt`/`CancelledError` (Ctrl+C) arrives — or any job raises — the handler cancels every still-running task and then **awaits those cancellations** (`gather(..., return_exceptions=True)`). Awaiting the cancelled tasks is what lets each job's `finally` blocks and `async with` cleanup actually execute before the original exception is re-raised. A bare `raise` propagates the original cause.\n\n## Verified Ctrl+C behavior (from the end-to-end run)\n\nWith 5 jobs and `max_concurrent=2`, sending SIGINT once produced:\n```\nstart 0\nstart 1\ncleanup 0      ← both started jobs' cleanup ran\ncleanup 1\nmain exiting: CancelledError\n```\nSo cleanup **does** run on interrupt. ✅ A second Ctrl+C forces an immediate exit (standard asyncio behavior).\n\n## Things worth knowing\n\n- **Fail-fast on errors:** if one job raises, the remaining jobs are cancelled (and cleaned up) and that original exception is re-raised. Jobs that were still waiting on the semaphore (never started) don't run their body/cleanup — there's nothing for them to clean up.\n- **`max_concurrent < 1`** raises `ValueError`.\n- The traceback you see on Ctrl+C (`CancelledError` → `KeyboardInterrupt`) is the standard `asyncio.run` output, not a bug. For a clean exit, wrap your entry point:\n  ```python\n  try:\n      asyncio.run(run_tasks(my_tasks, 4))\n  except (KeyboardInterrupt, asyncio.CancelledError):\n      pass\n  ```\n\n## Usage example\n```python\nimport asyncio\nfrom run import run_tasks\n\nasync def job(i):\n    async with resource(i):   # cleanup runs even on Ctrl+C\n        await do_work(i)\n\nasyncio.run(run_tasks([lambda i=i: job(i) for i in"}}

All 7 tests pass.\n\n## How it works\n\n- **Concurrency limit:** an `asyncio.Semaphore(max_concurrent)` gates each job. All jobs are scheduled up front and self-throttle by acquiring a slot, so at most `max_concurrent` run at once.\n- **Graceful interrupt (your main concern):** the jobs are awaited via `asyncio.gather`. When a `KeyboardInterrupt`/`CancelledError` (Ctrl+C) arrives — or any job raises — the handler cancels every still-running task and then **awaits those cancellations** (`gather(..., return_exceptions=True)`). Awaiting the cancelled tasks is what lets each job's `finally` blocks and `async with` cleanup actually execute before the original exception is re-raised. A bare `raise` propagates the original cause.\n\n## Verified Ctrl+C behavior (from the end-to-end run)\n\nWith 5 jobs and `max_concurrent=2`, sending SIGINT once produced:\n```\nstart 0\nstart 1\ncleanup 0      ← both started jobs' cleanup ran\ncleanup 1\nmain exiting: CancelledError\n```\nSo cleanup **does** run on interrupt. ✅ A second Ctrl+C forces an immediate exit (standard asyncio behavior).\n\n## Things worth knowing\n\n- **Fail-fast on errors:** if one job raises, the remaining jobs are cancelled (and cleaned up) and that original exception is re-raised. Jobs that were still waiting on the semaphore (never started) don't run their body/cleanup — there's nothing for them to clean up.\n- **`max_concurrent < 1`** raises `ValueError`.\n- The traceback you see on Ctrl+C (`CancelledError` → `KeyboardInterrupt`) is the standard `asyncio.run` output, not a bug. For a clean exit, wrap your entry point:\n  ```python\n  try:\n      asyncio.run(run_tasks(my_tasks, 4))\n  except (KeyboardInterrupt, asyncio.CancelledError):\n      pass\n  ```\n\n## Usage example\n```python\nimport asyncio\nfrom run import run_tasks\n\nasync def job(i):\n    async with resource(i):   # cleanup runs even on Ctrl+C\n        await do_work(i)\n\nasyncio.run(run_tasks([lambda i=i: job(i) for i in range(100)], max_concurrent=8))\n```\n\nRun the tests anytime with: `python3 /app/test_run.py`"}}
